message.content:
**CPU usage** refers to the amount of processing power your computer’s central‑processing units (CPUs) are currently consuming relative to their total capacity.  
It’s usually expressed as a percentage:

| Metric | What it shows |
|--------|---------------|
| **%usr** | Time spent executing user processes (your applications). |
| **%sys** | Time spent running kernel/system code. |
| **%idle** | Time when the CPU was idle – i.e., doing nothing useful. |
| **%iowait** | Time waiting for I/O operations (disk/network). |

---

### How to view CPU usage

#### On Linux / macOS

```bash
top          # interactive real‑time display
htop         # nicer interface (if installed)
mpstat -P ALL 1   # per‑core stats each second
```

`ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head` will list the top consumers at once.

#### On Windows

Open Task Manager → Performance tab → “CPU” section.  
Or use PowerShell:

```powershell
Get-Counter '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time'
```

#### In scripts/programs

*Python*

```python
import psutil
print(psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1))      # overall %
print([p.percent for p in psutil.process_iter(['name', 'percent'])])  # per process
```

*Bash shell script*

```bash
#!/bin/bash
while true; do
    uptime | awk '{print $NF}'            # load average
    mpstat 1 1 | grep -E '^Average'       # %idle etc.
done
```

---

### Interpreting values

| Usage range | Typical meaning |
|-------------|------------------|
| < 10 %     | Idle or light work |
| 10–50 %    | Normal multitasking |
| > 70 %     | Heavy workload or bottleneck |
| ~100 %     | Fully saturated (may cause lag) |

If one core consistently stays near 100 %, consider closing heavy apps, upgrading hardware, or checking for runaway processes (`kill`, `nice`, etc.).
